newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Lenin industry dying too, 73 years after his death.
newsitem.headline: Lenin industry dying too, 73 years after his death.

text.p: Before he died 73 years ago on Tuesday, Vladimir Lenin asked for the simplest of memorials.

Instead his death from a stroke at the age of 53 gave birth to a Leninist cult and to an industry turning out thousands of likenesses of the Bolshevik leader, complete with trademark goatee and flat cap, for town squares across the Soviet Union.

Only the collapse of communism in 1991 finally brought Lenin the posthumous personal obscurity he desired. But it also dealt a mortal blow to the "Lenin industry", leaving foundries and sculptors across Russia bereft of their favourite subject.
One such, is the Mytishchino Experimental Artistic Foundry on the northern outskirts of Moscow, where, on the 73rd anniversary of Lenin's passing, work is all but at a standstill.
"Times are very hard...We've not had one order for Lenin since 1991," plant director Vladimir Obleskov told Reuters on Monday. The workforce has dropped to 140 from 450 in 1991.
Out in the snow lie a couple of gigantic Lenin heads, one great bald dome sculpted in granite, the other in bronze, and a handful of Soviet heroes including a cosmonaut in his spacesuit.
They are virtually the only sign that this was once a thriving sculpture factory, turning out dozens of statues and busts at a time from blazing furnaces and frenetic workshops.

"Everything's collapsed, there's no life left in the place," mourned "Uncle Leon", one of the foundry's oldest employees, as he swept snow from the shattered remnants of the last great Lenin statue produced at Mytishchino -- left unpaid for in 1991.

Obleskov is anxious to play down the importance of Lenin -- only five percent of pre-1991 output was "political", he said. But economic crisis has relegated monuments of all sorts well down the list of priorities of city councils across Russia.
"People say to them 'How can you think about monuments when you can't even pay our pensions?'," Obleskov said.
The plant foreman, standing in a near-derelict workshop, bemoaned the loss of skills built up over decades and recalled fondly the days when six furnaces were in constant operation.

One of the senior foundrymen, at Mytishchino for 43 years, reminisced about the technological feat of installing Moscow's skyscraper-tall concrete and titanium statue of Yuri Gagarin, the first man in space, and the giant Lenin on October Square.

"I can't count how many Lenins I must have done. Every collective farm had one in those days," he said, adding that he had also worked on the coffin for Lenin's mummified corpse on Red Square and a sarcophagus for Vietnamese leader Ho Chi Minh.

It was prestigious work and foundry workers were rewarded with lavish parties on completion of major works. But it carried risks too, particularly under Josef Stalin, who founded the Lenin cult as a means of consolidating his own absolute power.
"We always had to take great care not to damage statues of Lenin or Stalin," the foreman said. Even today, neither he nor his workers are willing to give their names.
Defacing a statue of Lenin or Stalin, even accidentally, could mean a bullet in the head or a prison term in the GULag for foundrymen.

"There was a whole code of ethics about these statues," he foreman said. "We had to put them in place at midnight, with no one around to see Lenin or Stalin in chains. And we had to hoist them in a dignified way, not round the neck, for example."
Stalin statues were long since purged under the communists. Many Lenin monuments have now been removed, many of them smashed and defaced by angry mobs. Mytishchino's craftsmen disapprove.
"It's painful," the foreman said. "So, he made mistakes. But he earned his place in our history. People believed in him once. Now they say he's bad. But maybe one day he'll make a comeback."
